body: FLAG: free cash flow negative for years, about -$3.0 bn (2018) and -$3.27 bn (2019, 10-K), funded by junk bonds; cash content spending ~$14.6 bn vs only ~$9.2 bn of content amortisation in 2019, so reported profit overstated cash generation. Short sellers called it a debt-funded content treadmill. CONTEXT: (1) original content is a capital asset that builds a library and global brand; the gap between cash spend and amortisation was the growth investment; (2) subscribers and engagement grew globally with low churn, and prices could be raised; (3) content spend is a fixed cost spread over a growing base, so margins would rise with scale. FCF turned positive in 2020 (COVID production pause helped) and became large later as operating margin rose toward ~30% [post-2020 FCF levels from memory, unverified]. The stock still crashed -76% in 2021-22 on the first subscriber loss. LESSON: negative FCF is benign when the spend creates a durable asset that scales over a growing, retained customer base and the cash gap shrinks as a share of revenue; it is dangerous when the spend must rise faster than revenue just to stand still.

data.context: content library as capex; scale economics; pricing power; retention
data.lesson: track cash spend / revenue trend and retention

title: False alarm: Netflix's -$3.3 bn free cash flow
